meta.title: CS50 Problem Sets
meta.caveat: This is this repo's own _cs50psets pathway (a mix of CS50 AP-adapted and originally written problem sets), not Harvard's CS50 AP curriculum itself -- that's the separate cs50ap/cs50ap-extended carriers. Locators are this pathway's own order numbers (1-6), not CS50's own pset numbering. Readability's locator_slugs entry is a full external-looking path, not the /cs50-psets/ default, because that page's own permalink front matter deliberately mirrors CS50's own problems/2024/x/sentimental/readability slug.

alignment_log.scope: First pass, all 6 pset pages (mario-less, pathfinder, palindromes, square, caesar, readability) against all four frameworks
alignment_log.note: Transcribed from a prior hand-authored 'Standards Alignment' section already present on each page (2026-08-26 formula, done pset-by-pset against the working-in-python source repo's catalog files before this repo had its own carrier system). Every cited code re-confirmed against this repo's own _standards/*.json catalog copies. A code a page had flagged 'headers only' (present but not the point of the problem) is carried here as strength: related rather than strong.

2.1.note: Pathfinder: converting a two-digit hex byte into the character it represents, and back, is binary place-value one layer up -- hex digits are a compact stand-in for four bits at a time.

3.3.note: Readability: turning the Coleman-Liau formula into code is this in its most direct form.

3.4.note: Caesar and Readability walk a string one character at a time (rotating letters through ord()/chr(), or building up letter/word/sentence counts); Palindromes cleans a word down to its letters and compares it to its own reverse. All three treat a string as a sequence to be walked, not an opaque value.

3.5.note: Palindromes tests a word against its own reverse in one Boolean expression; Square tests whether a cell sits on the border the same way -- a Boolean expression doing work a nested conditional would do more verbosely.

3.6.note: Mario (less comfortable): the re-prompt loop until a valid height is entered.

3.7.note: Square: the border-cell test reads like a nested condition even though it's written as a single Boolean expression -- present in spirit, not in the code's actual structure.

3.8.note: Mario's pyramid, Square's grid, Caesar's letter shift, and Readability's character scan are all iteration doing the actual work of the problem, not incidental to it.

3.9.note: Mario (less comfortable): building the pyramid row by row is a small case of start-rough-then-refine. Palindromes: same, in miniature. Neither problem's real point is algorithm development -- it's a side effect of how the solution reads.

3.13.note: Pathfinder's optional helper function ('To Get Full Credit') is the thinnest instance -- headers only there. Square and Readability require a real helper function per sub-task; Caesar's shift-as-argument is the same decomposition idea applied to a command-line parameter.

5.6.note: Caesar: the cipher is a case study for why a tiny keyspace makes an encryption scheme breakable, even though the exam itself doesn't test encryption mechanics.

9-12.AP.14.note: Mario, Palindromes, Square, and Readability all turn on a deliberate control-structure choice (loop vs. conditional vs. helper function) made concrete in each solution.

9-12.AP.16.note: Square and Readability both require breaking the problem into named, reusable functions rather than one long script.

9-12.DA.8.note: Pathfinder and Caesar both convert between a character and a numeric representation of it -- the same letter can be written as a symbol or as a number, and moving between the two is the whole point of each problem.

9-12.NI.6.note: Caesar's own cipher, and why a small keyspace makes it breakable, is a direct case study for this standard.

HS-ALG-PS-02.note: Every pset in this pathway is, at bottom, an algorithmic problem broken into steps and translated into code -- this is the one standard all six currently share.

HS-DAT-DC-24.note: Mario (less comfortable): the re-prompt loop is range-checking in practice -- is the value the right type, does it fall in a sensible range.

HS-PRO-PD-12.note: Square and Readability both require decomposing the problem into a helper function per sub-task rather than inlining everything.

HS-SYS-SE-33.note: Caesar's cipher is a case study in a system (the encryption scheme) whose security depends on its keyspace.

C2.2.note: Caesar: headers only -- the cipher touches basic security concepts without the problem asking students to reason about them directly.

C4.4.note: Pathfinder and Caesar both convert data between representations (hex byte to character, letter to shift number) -- data has types, and those types get encoded in specific ways.

C4.9.note: Mario, Palindromes, Square, Caesar, and Readability all lean on the same programming toolkit (loops, conditionals, functions with parameters) this standard names.

C5.4.note: Square: running check50 against a solution makes testing a distinct, visible step rather than an afterthought.
